hook: Why does burning methane release so much energy, while splitting water takes so much? You can predict it with a pencil: count the bonds that break, count the bonds that form, and look up how strong each one is. The answer comes out within a few percent of what a calorimeter measures.

prereq.q: The bond energy of a covalent bond is
options: the energy needed to break it
the energy released when it breaks
prereq.why: It is the depth of the potential energy well: the energy needed to pull the bonded atoms apart.

prereq.q: How many bonds are in one CO₂ molecule (O=C=O)?
prereq.why: The Lewis structure has carbon double-bonded to each oxygen.

prereq.q: ΔH for a thermochemical equation is per
prereq.why: It goes with the coefficients exactly as written.

figure.caption: Breaking the reactant bonds absorbs energy (up); forming the product bonds releases energy (down). The net change is ΔH.

chain.effect: breaking a bond absorbs energy, its bond enthalpy (always positive)

chain.cause: Separate atoms are pulled together into a bond
chain.effect: forming the bond releases the same amount of energy

chain.cause: A reaction breaks the reactant bonds and forms the product bonds
Strong bonds form from weak ones
chain.effect: more energy is released than absorbed: exothermic

chain.cause: Table values are averages over many molecules
chain.effect: the result is an estimate, close to but not equal to the measured ΔH

ideas: A bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break 1 mol of a bond in gas-phase molecules; it is always positive.
ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Broken first; this is not "products minus reactants".
Draw the structures and count every bond, including coefficients: 2 O₂ means 2 O=O.
Multiple bonds are stronger than single bonds between the same atoms.
Average values make the answer an estimate; it is meant for gas-phase reactions.

misconception.wrong: Energy is stored in chemical bonds and released when the bonds break.
misconception.right: Breaking a bond always absorbs energy. Energy is released when bonds form; a reaction is exothermic when the bonds formed are stronger overall than those broken.

summary: Bond enthalpies give an estimate of ΔH: add the bond enthalpies of the bonds broken, then subtract those of the bonds formed. Breaking bonds absorbs energy and forming them releases it, so a reaction that forms stronger bonds than it breaks is exothermic.
